'''broad-based''' (brâd′bāst), ''a.'' Having a broad foundation; securely founded. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Her throne . . .
''Broad-based'' upon her people’s will.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', To the Queen.}}}}

'''broadbill''' (brâd′bil), ''n.'' '''1.''' The shoveler-duck, ''Spatula clypeata.''—'''2.''' The spoonbill, ''Platalea leucorodia.''—'''3.''' The scaup-duck, ''Fuligula marila'', and other species of that genus.—'''4.''' A bird of the family ''Eurylæmidæ.'' There are nine or ten species of broadbills peculiar to the Indian region. Also called ''broadmouth.''

'''broad-billed''' (brâd′bild), ''a.'' In ''ornith.'', having a broad bill.—{{smaller|'''Broad-billed sandpiper,''' the ''Limicola platyrhyncha.''}}

'''broadbrim''' (brâd′brim), ''n.'' '''1.''' A hat with a very broad brim, especially the form of hat worn by members of the Society of Friends. Hence—'''2.''' A member of that society; a Quaker. ''Carlyle.'' [Colloq.]

'''broad-brimmed''' (brâd′brimd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having a broad border, brim, or edge.
{{smaller block|Govert Lockerman, without taking his pipe out of his mouth, turned up his eye from under his ''broad-brimmed'' hat to see who hailed him thus discourteously.
{{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 251.}}}}
'''2.''' Wearing a hat with a broad brim.
{{smaller block|This ''broad-brimm’d'' hawker of holy things.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, x.}}}}

'''broadcast''' (brâd′kȧst), ''a.'' '''1.''' Cast or dispersed
readings.c3s1:
¶
'''broaden''' (brâ′dn), ''v.'' [< ''broad'' + ''-en''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''broad'', ''v.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To grow broad or broader.
{{smaller block|To ''broaden'' into boundless day.
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, xcv.}}}}
'''II.''' ''trans.'' To make broad; increase in breadth; render more broad or comprehensive: as, “''broaden’d'' nostrils,” ''Thomson'', Winter.

'''broad-eyed''' (brâd′īd), ''a.'' Having a wide view or survey.

'''broad-fronted''' (brâd′frun″ted), ''a.'' Having a broad front; having a wide forehead: as, “''broad-fronted'' Cæsar,” ''Shak.'', A. and C., i. 5.

'''broad-gage''' (brâd′gāj), ''a.'' Having the space between the rails wider than the standard gage of 56½ inches: said of a railroad track: opposed to ''narrow-gage'', which signifies less than the standard width. See ''gage''<sup>2</sup>.

'''broadhorn''' (brâd′hôrn), ''n.'' A name by which the flat-boats on the Mississippi and other American rivers were formerly known.
{{smaller block|A ''broad-horn'', a prime river conveyance. {{right|''Irving.''}}
The river’s earliest commerce was in great barges,— keel-boats, ''broadhorns.''
{{right|''S. L. Clemens'', Life on the Mississippi, p. 41.}}}}

'''broad-horned''' (brâd′hôrnd), ''a.'' Having wide-spread horns. ''Huloet.''

'''broadleaf, broadleaf-tree''' (brâd′lēf, -trē), ''n.'' A tall tree, ''Terminalia latifolia'', natural order ''Combretaceæ'', common in Jamaica, bearing large and long-petioled leaves at the end of the branches.

'''broadly''' (brâd′li), ''adv.'' '''1.''' In a broad manner.
{{smaller block|That ''broadly'' flows through Pylos’ fields.
{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, v.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|broad|689|broadside}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|He grins, and looks ''broad'' nonsense with a stare.
{{right|''Pope'', Dunciad, ii. 194.}}}}
'''6.''' Widely diffused; open; full: as, in ''broad'' sunshine; ''broad'' daylight.
{{smaller block|Ful oft, whan it is ''brode'' day.
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., ii. 107.}}}}
{{smaller block|I count little of the many things I see pass at ''broad'' noonday, in large and open streets.
{{right|''Sterne'', Sentimental Journey, p. 103.}}}}
{{smaller block|It was ''broad'' day, and the people, recovered from their panic, were enabled to see and estimate the force of the enemy. {{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 32.}}}}
'''7.''' Unconfined; free; unrestrained. {{smaller|(''a'') Used absolutely.}}
{{smaller block|As ''broad'' and general as the casing air.
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Unrestrained by a sense of propriety or fitness; unpolished; loutish.}}
{{smaller block|Tell him his pranks have been too ''broad'' to bear with.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') Unrestrained by considerations of decency; indelicate; indecent.}}
{{smaller block|As chaste and modest as he is esteemed, it cannot be denied but in some places he is ''broad'' and fulsome.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Juvenal’s Satires, Ded.}}}}
{{smaller|(''d'') Unrestrained by fear or caution; bold; unreserved.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>For from ''broad'' words, and ’cause he fail’d
His presence at the tyrant’s feast, I hear,
Macduff lives in disgrace. ''Shak.'', Macbeth, iii. 6.</poem>}}
'''8.''' Characterized by a full, strong utterance; coarsely vigorous; not weak or slender in sound: as, ''broad'' Scotch; ''broad'' Doric; a ''broad'' vowel, such as ''ä'' or ''â'' or ''ō''.—'''9†.''' Plain; evident.
{{smaller block|Proves thee far and wide a ''broad'' goose.
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 4.}}}} 10. In the ''fine arts'', characterized by breadth: as, a picture remarkable for the ''broad'' treatment of its subject. See ''breadth'', 3.—'''As broad as (it is) long''', {{smaller|equal upon the whole; the same either way.}}
{{smaller block|It is ''as broad as long'' whether they rise to others or bring others down to them.
{{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange.''}}}}
{{smaller|'''Broad Church''', the popular designation of a party in the Church of England. See ''Episcopalian''.—'''Broad folio, broad quarto''', etc., names given to drawing-paper folded the broadest way.—'''Broad gage.''' See ''gage''<sup>2</sup>.—'''Broad glass,''' window-glass of a cheap quality formed by blowing a long cylinder, cutting it apart, and allowing the pieces to soften and flatten out in a kiln.}}
{{img float|file=century v01 p0715 c1f1.png|width=161px|align=left|cap={{smaller|Broad Pennant of a Commodore, United States Navy.}}}} {{smaller|See ''glass''. Also called ''British sheet-glass'', ''cylinder-glass'', ''German plate-glass'', and ''spread window-glass''.—'''Broad lace,''' a woolen fabric made in bands about 4 inches wide, and used as an ornamental border to the upholstery of a carriage.   ''Car-builder’s Dict.''—'''Broad pennant''' (''naut.''), a swallow-tailed flag carried at the mast-head of a man-of-war as the distinctive mark of a commodore.}} ='''Syn. 1.''' Extended, spread.—'''1''' and '''2.''' ''Wide'', ''Broad''. See ''wide''.—'''7.''' (''c'') Vulgar, obscene.

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A shallow, fenny lake formed by the expansion of a river over adjacent flat land covered more or less with a reedy growth; a flooded fen, or lake in a fen: as, the Norfolk ''broads.'' [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|A ''broad'' is the spread of a river into a sheet of water, which is certainly neither lake nor lagoon.
{{right|''Southey'', Letters (1812), II. 307.}}}}
{{smaller block|Then across the mill-pool, and through the deep crooks, out into the ''broads'', and past the withered beds of weeds which told of coming winter.
{{right|''H. Kingsley'', Ravenshoe, viii.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''mech.'', a tool used for turning down the insides and bottoms of cylinders in the lathe.—'''3.''' An English coin first issued in 1619 by James I., and worth at the time 20''s.'' {{img float|file=century v01 p0715 c1f2.png|width=203px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Reverse.}} {{smaller|Broad of James I., British Museum. (Size of the original.)}}}} 44 The coin was also issued subsequently. Also called ''laurel'' and ''broad-piece.''

'''broad''' (brâd), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''broode, brode,'' < AS. ''brāde'' (= MHG. ''breite,'' G. ''breit''), broadly; from the adj.]   '''1†.''' Broadly; openly; plainly.
{{smaller block|Crist spak himself ful ''broode'' in holy writ.
{{right|''Chaucer,'' Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 739.}}}}
'''2†.''' Widely; copiously; abundantly.   ''Chaucer.'' —'''3.''' Broadly; fully.
{{smaller block|With all his crimes ''broad'' blown, as flush as May.
{{right|''Shak.,'' Hamlet, iii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Lying ''broad'' awake I thought of you and Effie dear.
{{right|''Tennyson,'' May Queen (Conclusion).}}}}

'''broad†''', ''v. t.''   [ME. ''broden,'' < AS. ''brādian,'' spread, < ''brād,'' broad. Cf. ''bread''<sup>2</sup>.]   To make broad; spread.
{{smaller block|Tyll the blessed bredd [bird] ''brodid'' his wingis.
{{right|''Richard the Redeless.''}}}}

'''broad-arrow''' (brâd′ar″ō), ''n.''   [< ME. ''brode arow, brodarwe,'' etc., a heavy arrow; < ''broad'' + ''arrow.'']   {{img float|file=century v01 p0715 c2f1.png|width=90px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Broad-arrow.}}}} The royal mark of British government stores of every description, which it is felony to obliterate or deface. {{smaller|Persons unlawfully in possession of goods marked with the broad-arrow forfeit the goods and are subject to a penalty of £200. The ''broad-arrow'' was the cognizance of Henry, Viscount Sydney, Earl of Romney, Master-general of Ordnance from 1693 to 1702, and was first used in his time. In heraldry it differs from the pheon (which see) in having the inside of the barbs plain.}}

'''broadax''' (brâd′aks), ''n.''   [< ME. ''brodax, broodaxe,'' etc., < AS. ''brādæx,'' < ''brād,'' broad, + ''æx,'' ax: see ''broad'' and ''ax''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1†.''' A battle-ax.—'''2.''' An ax with a broad edge, for hewing timber. See cut under ''ax''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then let the sounds of measured stroke
And grating saw begin,
The ''broad-axe'' to the gnarled oak,
The mallet to the pin!</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', Ship-Builders.}}}}

'''broad-based''' (brâd′bāst), ''a.'' Having a broad foundation; securely founded. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Her throne . . .
''Broad-based'' upon her people’s will.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', To the Queen.}}}}

Also called ''broadmouth.''

'''broad-billed''' (brâd′bild), ''a.'' In ''ornith.'', having a broad bill.—{{smaller|'''Broad-billed sandpiper,''' the ''Limicola platyrhyncha.''}}

'''broadbrim''' (brâd′brim), ''n.'' '''1.''' A hat with a very broad brim, especially the form of hat worn by members of the Society of Friends. Hence—'''2.''' A member of that society; a Quaker.   ''Carlyle.'' [Colloq.]

'''broad-brimmed''' (brâd′brimd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having a broad border, brim, or edge.
{{smaller block|Govert Lockerman, without taking his pipe out of his mouth, turned up his eye from under his ''broad-brimmed'' hat to see who hailed him thus discourteously.
{{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 251.}}}}
'''2.''' Wearing a hat with a broad brim.
{{smaller block|This ''broad-brimm’d'' hawker of holy things.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, x.}}}}

'''broadcast''' (brâd′kȧst), ''a.'' '''1.''' Cast or dispersed upon the ground with the hand, as seed in sowing: opposed to sowed in drills or rows.—'''2.''' Widely spread or diffused.

'''broadcast''' (brâd′kȧst), ''n.'' In ''agri.'', a method of sowing in which the seed is thrown from the hand in handfuls.
{{smaller block|<poem>My lads, said he, let ''broad-cast'' be,
And come away to drill.</poem>
{{right|''Hood.''}}}}

'''broadcast''' (brâd′kȧst), ''adv.'' '''1.''' By scattering or throwing at large from the hand: as, to sow ''broadcast.''—'''2.''' So as to disseminate widely; in wide dissemination.
{{smaller block|An impure, so called, literature sown ''broadcast'' over the land.
{{right|''Blackwood’s Mag.''}}}}

'''broadcloth''' (brâd′klôth), ''n.'' A fine woolen cloth, commonly black, with a finished surface, mostly used in making men’s garments: so called from its breadth, which is usually 60 inches.
{{smaller block|Every whole woollen cloth, called ''broad cloth'', which shall be made and set to sale after the feast called St. Peter ad vincula, which shall be in the year of our Lord M.CCCC.LXV., after the full watering, racking, straining, or tenturing of the same, ready to sale, shall hold and contain in length xxiv yards, and to every yard an inch, containing the breadth of a man’s thumb, to be measured by the crest of the same cloth, and in breadth ij yards, or vij quarters at the least, within the lists.
{{right|''English Gilds'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 351, note.}}}}
{{smaller block|They be all patched cloutes and ragges, in comparison of faire wouen ''broade cloathes.''
{{right|''Ascham'', The Scholemaster, p. 60.}}}}

'''broaden''' (brâ′dn), ''v.''   [< ''broad'' + ''-en''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''broad'', ''v.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To grow broad or broader.
{{smaller block|To ''broaden'' into boundless day.
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, xcv.}}}}
'''II.''' ''trans.'' To make broad; increase in breadth; render more broad or comprehensive: as, “''broaden’d'' nostrils,” ''Thomson'', Winter.

'''broad-eyed''' (brâd′īd), ''a.'' Having a wide view or survey.

'''broad-fronted''' (brâd′frun″ted), ''a.'' Having a broad front; having a wide forehead: as, “''broad-fronted'' Cæsar,” ''Shak.'', A. and C., i. 5.

'''broad-gage''' (brâd′gāj), ''a.'' Having the space between the rails wider than the standard gage of 56½ inches: said of a railroad track: opposed to ''narrow-gage'', which signifies less than the standard width. See ''gage''<sup>2</sup>.

'''broadhorn''' (brâd′hôrn), ''n.'' A name by which the flat-boats on the Mississippi and other American rivers were formerly known.
{{smaller block|A ''broad-horn'', a prime river conveyance. {{right|''Irving.''}}}}
{{smaller block|The river’s earliest commerce was in great barges,— keel-boats, ''broadhorns.''
{{right|''S. L. Clemens'', Life on the Mississippi, p. 41.}}}}

'''broad-horned''' (brâd′hôrnd), ''a.'' Having wide-spread horns.   ''Huloet.''

'''broadleaf, broadleaf-tree''' (brâd′lēf, -trē), ''n.'' A tall tree, ''Terminalia latifolia'', natural order ''Combretaceæ'', common in Jamaica, bearing large and long-petioled leaves at the end of the branches.

'''broadly''' (brâd′li), ''adv.'' '''1.''' In a broad manner.
{{smaller block|That ''broadly'' flows through Pylos’ fields.
{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, v.}}}}
{{smaller block|Custine has spoken out more ''broadly''.
{{right|''Burke'', Present State of Affairs.}}}}
{{smaller block|These simple, ''broadly'' draped figures were sculptured by Niccola at Pisa.
{{right|''C. C. Perkins'', Italian Sculpture, p. 21.}}}}
Specifically—'''2.''' In ''zoöl.'', so as to extend over a relatively large space: as, ''broadly'' emarginate; ''broadly'' bisinuate, etc. A part is ''broadly'' truncate when the truncation is nearly or quite equal to its greatest width.

'''broadmouth''' (brâd′mouth), ''n.'' A bird of the family ''Eurylæmidæ'' (which see); a broadbill.

'''broadness''' (brâd′nes), ''n.''   [< ''broad'' + ''-ness''.]   '''1.''' Breadth; extent from side to side.—'''2.''' Coarseness; grossness; indelicacy.
{{smaller block|''Broadness'' and indecency of allusion.
{{right|''Craik'', Eng. Lit., i. 524.}}}}

'''broad-piece''' (brâd′pēs), ''n.'' Same as ''broad'', ''n.'', 3.

'''broad-seal''' (brâd′sēl), ''n.'' The official or great seal of a country or state: as, “the king’s ''broad-seal'',” ''Sheldon'', Miracles, p. 61. [More correctly as two words.]—{{smaller|'''Broad-seal war''', in ''U. S. hist.'', a contest in the House of Representatives, in December, 1839, as to the admission or exclusion of five Whig members from New Jersey, who had certificates of election under the broad seal of the State, but whose seats were contested by Democratic claimants.}}

'''broad-seal''' (brâd′sēl), ''v. t.''   [< ''broad-seal'', ''n.'']   To stamp as with the broad seal; guarantee; make sure.
{{smaller block|Thy presence ''broad-seals'' our delights for pure.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, v. 3.}}}}

'''broad-shouldered''' (brâd′shōl″dėrd), ''a.'' Having the back broad across the shoulders.
{{smaller block|''Broad-shouldered'', and his arms were round and long.
{{right|''Dryden''.}}}}

'''broadside''' (brâd′sīd), ''n.'' '''1.''' The whole side of a ship above the water-line, from the bow to the quarter.—'''2.''' A simultaneous discharge of all the guns on one side of a vessel of war: as, to fire a ''broadside.''—'''3.''' In general, any comprehensive attack with weapons of any kind directed against one point or object.
{{smaller block|Give him a ''broadside'', my brave boys, with your pikes.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, v. 4.}}}}
'''4.''' A sheet printed on one side only, and without arrangement in columns; especially, such a sheet containing some item of news, or an attack upon some person, etc., and designed for distribution.
{{smaller block|Every member of the convention received a copy of this draft of a constitution, printed on ''broadsides'' in large type. {{right|''Bancroft'', Hist. Const., I. 119.}}}}
{{smaller block|Van Citters gives the best account of the trial. I have seen a ''broadside'' which confirms his narrative.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., vi., note.}}}}
'''5.''' Any surface resembling the side of a ship in breadth, etc., as a house-front.
{{smaller block|In the great, blank, gray ''broadside'', there were only four windows. {{right|''Dickens.''}}}}
'''Broadside on''', {{smaller|with the side in advance; sidewise.}}—'''To take on the broadside''', {{smaller|to treat freely and unceremoniously.}}
{{smaller block|Determined to ''take'' the world ''on the broadside'', and eat thereof, and be filled. {{right|''Carlyle'', Diderot.}}}}

'''broadside''' (brâd′sīd), ''adv.''   [< ''broadside'', ''n.'']   '''1.''' With the broadside directed toward the point specified.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
